etymology: From the Old French brigandine, the body-armour worn by the brigand or foot-soldier — small iron plates or scales quilted between layers of cloth or leather. The Authorized translators used it for the Hebrew siryōn, the scale-coat or coat of mail.
biblical_def: A brigandine is the scale-coat — a corselet of small overlapping iron plates sewn upon leather, the heaviest defence a man of war could carry upon his body. The word stands twice in the Authorized Version, and both times it stands in a scene of doom. Jeremiah mocks Egypt mustering at Carchemish: “Harness the horses; and get up, ye horsemen, and stand forth with your helmets; furbish the spears, and put on the brigandines” (Jer 46:4). Every piece is in place, the plates are buckled, the spears are burnished — and the LORD has already appointed the day of slaughter. So also against Babylon: “against him that lifteth himself up in his brigandine: and spare ye not her young men” (Jer 51:3). The scale-coat is not proof against a decree of God. The lesson was written once in blood at Ramoth-gilead, where a bow drawn at a venture found Ahab “between the joints of the harness” (1Ki 22:34) — the one seam armour cannot cover, and the exact seam the arrow of providence was aimed at. Yet Scripture does not leave the believer unarmoured. What the brigandine could not do, the LORD Himself has done: “he put on righteousness as a breastplate, and an helmet of salvation upon his head” (Isa 59:17), and that same panoply He gives to His people, bidding them “put on the whole armour of God” (Eph 6:11). Iron scales rust and split; the righteousness of Christ never fails.
webster_summary: A coat of mail; ancient body-armour of small iron plates quilted upon cloth or leather.
webster_full: BRIGANDINE, a coat of mail; armour for the body, formed of small plates of iron sewed upon quilted linen or leather.
From the Old French brigandine, the harness of the brigand or light foot-soldier.
It renders the Hebrew siryōn, elsewhere Englished habergeon and coat of mail.
Jeremiah bids Egypt put on the brigandines — in irony, on the day of her slaughter (Jer 46:4).
The word names the strongest defence a man could wear, and its uselessness against God.
scriptures: Jer 46:4
Harness the horses; and get up, ye horsemen, and stand forth with your helmets; furbish the spears, and put on the brigandines.
Jer 51:3
Against him that bendeth let the archer bend his bow, and against him that lifteth himself up in his brigandine: and spare ye not her young men; destroy ye utterly all her host.
For he put on righteousness as a breastplate, and an helmet of salvation upon his head; and he put on the garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a cloke.
Eph 6:11
Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.
corruption_summary: A plain archaic word for the coat of mail; the live corruption is the modern brigandine of self-made security worn against the judgment of God.
corruption_paragraphs: The word has faded, but the folly it exposes is perennial. Men still buckle on defences against the day of the LORD: the funded account, the clean record, the reputation for decency, the church membership carried like a plate of iron over the chest. Egypt furbished her spears and put on her brigandines and was broken all the same, for no armour turns a decree of heaven. This is exactly the confidence Scripture strips: “There is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against the LORD” (Pro 21:30). The man who trusts his own covering has mistaken the nature of the battle; his enemy is not a Chaldean archer but the holy God whose law he has broken, and against that adversary a scale-coat of moral respectability is thinner than paper.

The principle to recover is that God supplies the only armour that holds, and He supplies it in His Son. Isaiah sees the LORD arming Himself — righteousness for a breastplate, salvation for a helmet — and the astonishing gospel is that the armour the Warrior wore He now clothes His people with. Paul's panoply in Ephesians 6 is not a set of virtues the Christian manufactures but the whole equipment of Christ imputed and imparted: His righteousness on the breast, His salvation on the head, His truth about the loins, His gospel underfoot. The brigandine had a seam, and an arrow shot at a venture found it. The armour of God has none, because it is Christ Himself, and He cannot be pierced by any charge the law or the devil can bring.
roots_summary: Brigandine = the scale-coat of iron plates, the soldier's heaviest body-armour.
roots_lines: Brigandine — Old French, the mail-coat of the brigand or foot-soldier.
Hebrew siryōn, the scale-armour, elsewhere rendered habergeon or coat of mail.
Twice in the Authorized Version, both times in an oracle of doom (Jer 46:4; Jer 51:3).
Ahab died of an arrow that found the joint of the harness (1Ki 22:34).
Its counterpart in grace is the whole armour of God (Eph 6:11).
usage: Put on the brigandines — and be broken anyway, for the LORD had appointed the day.
Every brigandine has a seam; the righteousness of Christ has none.
A man may be armed to the throat and still be naked before God.

etymology: From the Middle Dutch bolwerc, “plank-work” (bole, a tree-trunk, + werk, work) — a rampart or siege-work of timber and earth. In the Authorized Version it renders both the mound thrown up against a city and the defensive work that guards one.
biblical_def: A bulwark is a rampart — a work of timber, earth, and stone raised either to batter a city or to defend it. Scripture uses the word both ways, and the double use is instructive. In the law of siege Israel is told to spare the fruit trees and take the rest: “thou shalt build bulwarks against the city that maketh war with thee, until it be subdued” (Deu 20:20). The Preacher shows the same works in a parable of forgotten wisdom: “there came a great king against it, and besieged it, and built great bulwarks against it” (Ecc 9:14), and a poor wise man delivered the city, and no man remembered him. But the word rises to its glory in the Psalms and in Isaiah. The sons of Korah bid the pilgrim walk the circuit of Zion and take her measure: “Mark ye well her bulwarks, consider her palaces; that ye may tell it to the generation following” (Psa 48:13). The stones are to be counted not for pride in masonry but for testimony — this is what the LORD has kept. And Isaiah takes the last step, dissolving the masonry into the LORD Himself: “We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks” (Isa 26:1). The church's true defence is not her structures but her Saviour.
webster_summary: A rampart; a fortification of earth and timber, raised either to defend a place or to besiege one.
webster_full: BULWARK, a bastion or rampart; a fortification; that which secures against an enemy or an assault.
From the Dutch bolwerc, plank-work — a work of tree-trunks and earth.
In Scripture it names both the besieger's mound (Deu 20:20; Ecc 9:14) and the city's defence (Psa 48:13).
Figuratively, whatever stands as a strong protection: a bulwark of the truth.
Isaiah appoints salvation itself for walls and bulwarks (Isa 26:1).
scriptures: Only the trees which thou knowest that they be not trees for meat, thou shalt destroy and cut them down; and thou shalt build bulwarks against the city that maketh war with thee, until it be subdued.
Mark ye well her bulwarks, consider her palaces; that ye may tell it to the generation following.
Isa 26:1
In that day shall this song be sung in the land of Judah; We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks.
Ecc 9:14
There was a little city, and few men within it; and there came a great king against it, and besieged it, and built great bulwarks against it:
corruption_summary: The church is still told to mark her bulwarks; the corruption is the age's contempt for boundaries, creeds, and walls of any kind.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct is that a wall is an insult and a boundary a failure of love, so every bulwark the church ever raised is treated as an embarrassment to be quietly dismantled: the confession, the membership roll, the fenced table, the elders' oversight, the discipline that puts an unrepentant man outside the camp. The dismantlers call it openness; Scripture calls it the breaching of a city. Solomon knew what a man without walls becomes: “He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls” (Pro 25:28). A congregation that will not name a doctrine, guard a table, or bar a wolf has not become generous; it has become indefensible, and the first serious siege will prove it.

The recovery is a right ordering of the two things Psalm 48 and Isaiah 26 hold together. Mark the bulwarks — walk them, count them, teach them to the generation following — for the visible church really does have walls, and the 1689 Confession, the ordinances rightly fenced, and a plurality of faithful elders are among them. But never mistake the masonry for the security. Isaiah appoints salvation itself for walls and bulwarks: the city stands because God has undertaken for it, not because the stones are thick. So the psalmist ends his circuit of Zion not with a boast about towers but with a confession: “this God is our God for ever and ever: he will be our guide even unto death” (Psa 48:14). Guard the walls; trust the LORD of the walls.
roots_summary: Bulwark = a rampart of timber and earth — the siege-mound raised against a city, or the defence that guards it.
roots_lines: Bulwark — Middle Dutch bolwerc, “plank-work”: tree-trunks and earth.
Offensive sense: the mound built against a besieged city (Deu 20:20; Ecc 9:14).
Defensive sense: the ramparts of Zion, to be marked and told to the next generation (Psa 48:13).
Isaiah dissolves the masonry into the Saviour: salvation for walls and bulwarks (Isa 26:1).
The figure passes into English for any strong protection of truth or liberty.
usage: Mark ye well her bulwarks — count the stones, then tell the children why they stand.
A church that dismantles every bulwark has not grown generous; it has grown indefensible.
Salvation for walls and bulwarks: the city is safe because God has undertaken for it.

etymology: From batter, to beat down (Old French batre, from Latin battuere), and ram, the butting male sheep whose head the engine's iron cap imitated. It renders the Hebrew kar, the siege-engine swung against a wall or gate.
biblical_def: The battering ram is the great swung beam, iron-headed, hung in a frame and driven against a city's wall or gate until the masonry gives. It belongs to the full apparatus of ancient siege — the mount cast up, the fort built, the camp set, the engines brought forward — and Ezekiel is the prophet who names it. In his sign-act against Jerusalem the LORD commands him to build the whole siege in miniature upon a tile: “lay siege against it, and build a fort against it, and cast a mount against it; set the camp also against it, and set battering rams against it round about” (Eze 4:2). The child's model was a prophecy, and it came literally to pass. Later Ezekiel watches Nebuchadnezzar at the parting of the way, shaking his arrows and consulting his idols, and the lot falls upon Jerusalem: it is “to appoint battering rams against the gates, to cast a mount, and to build a fort” (Eze 21:22). Mark what that verse teaches. The heathen king thought he was reading omens; in truth the divination fell out as it did because the LORD had appointed Jerusalem for judgment. The ram against the gate was swung by Chaldean arms, but it was aimed by the God whose covenant Judah had broken. Tyre learned the same: “he shall set engines of war against thy walls” (Eze 26:9).
webster_summary: An ancient military engine — an iron-headed beam swung to beat down the walls or gates of a besieged city.
webster_full: BATTERING RAM, an engine of war used before the invention of cannon, to beat down the walls of besieged places.
A long beam, armed at the end with iron formed like a ram's head, suspended and swung against the wall.
From batter, to beat with successive blows, and ram, from the butting animal it resembled.
Hebrew kar; part of the siege apparatus with the mount, the fort, and the camp (Eze 4:2).
Nebuchadnezzar's divination appointed battering rams against the gates of Jerusalem (Eze 21:22).
scriptures: Eze 4:2
And lay siege against it, and build a fort against it, and cast a mount against it; set the camp also against it, and set battering rams against it round about.

At his right hand was the divination for Jerusalem, to appoint captains, to open the mouth in the slaughter, to lift up the voice with shouting, to appoint battering rams against the gates, to cast a mount, and to build a fort.
Eze 26:9
And he shall set engines of war against thy walls, and with his axes he shall break down thy towers.

Behold the mounts, they are come unto the city to take it; and the city is given into the hand of the Chaldeans, that fight against it, because of the sword, and of the famine, and of the pestilence: and what thou hast spoken is come to pass; and, behold, thou seest it.
corruption_summary: A piece of siege realia; the live misuse is the modern habit of calling every hard providence an assault and never asking what wall God is breaking down.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. A battering ram is a battering ram; no movement is contending for the word. But there is a live misuse of the picture, and it is common in the pew. When the blows fall — the diagnosis, the loss, the years of unanswered prayer — the instinctive reading is that the enemy is at the gate and nothing more, and the whole business of the soul becomes resisting the siege. Ezekiel forbids so thin a reading. The rams that broke Jerusalem were swung by Chaldeans, but they were appointed by the LORD against a city that had spurned His covenant and stoned His prophets, and the man who saw only Nebuchadnezzar saw nothing.

The principle to recover is that God governs the siege-works of His own providence, and He aims them at what must come down. He is not petty and He is not cruel; He is the surgeon who breaks a wall to reach a citizen. The Christian under hard blows is therefore to ask, not merely how to endure, but what proud tower is being battered and what the LORD means to build in its room — for “whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth” (Heb 12:6). And there is a mercy in the picture that the besieged never had: the wall God batters in His children is not the soul itself but the works of the flesh entrenched in it, and when the breach is made, it is Christ who comes in through it.
roots_summary: Battering ram = the iron-headed beam swung against a city wall; Hebrew kar, part of the full siege-work.
roots_lines: Battering ram — batter (Latin battuere, to beat) + ram, for its iron ram's-head cap.
Hebrew kar; named with the mount, the fort, and the camp of a full siege (Eze 4:2).
Ezekiel built the whole siege in miniature on a tile as a sign against Jerusalem.
Nebuchadnezzar's omens appointed the rams — but the LORD appointed the omens (Eze 21:22).
Tyre met the same engines of war against her walls (Eze 26:9).
usage: Set battering rams against it round about — a prophet's tile that came literally true.
The Chaldean swung the ram; the LORD aimed it.
Ask not only how to endure the blows, but what wall God intends to bring down.

etymology: From foot and man — a soldier who serves on foot, as distinguished from the horseman and the charioteer. It renders the Hebrew raglī, “one on foot,” and in one place the royal runners or guardsmen.
biblical_def: A footman in the Authorized Version is not a servant in livery but an infantryman — the soldier who marches and fights on his own two feet, counted by the hundred thousand in Israel's musters. Moses reckons the nation at “six hundred thousand footmen” (Num 11:21); Israel assembles “four hundred thousand footmen that drew sword” (Jdg 20:2); and when the ark was taken there fell of Israel “thirty thousand footmen” (1Sa 4:10). The footman is the common man of the host, the rank the LORD most often used and most often thinned. But the word receives its enduring weight from a single question the LORD puts to a weary prophet. Jeremiah had complained of the men of Anathoth who sought his life, and the answer he got was not comfort but a harder charge: “If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? and if in the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee, then how wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan?” (Jer 12:5). Here is the whole doctrine of Christian endurance in one verse. The footrace is the light trial; the horses and the flooded Jordan are what is coming. God does not answer weariness by lowering the course — He answers it by strengthening the runner for a heavier one.
webster_summary: A soldier who marches and fights on foot; an infantryman, as opposed to a horseman.
webster_full: FOOTMAN, a soldier who marches and fights on foot; foot-soldier; infantry.
From foot and man; Hebrew raglī, one who goes on foot.
In the Authorized Version it is a military word, not the later English sense of a liveried servant.
Israel's musters are counted in footmen — six hundred thousand at Sinai (Num 11:21).
Jeremiah is asked how he will contend with horses if footmen have wearied him (Jer 12:5).
scriptures: Jer 12:5

If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? and if in the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee, then how wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan?
And Moses said, The people, among whom I am, are six hundred thousand footmen; and thou hast said, I will give them flesh, that they may eat a whole month.
Jdg 20:2
And the chief of all the people, even of all the tribes of Israel, presented themselves in the assembly of the people of God, four hundred thousand footmen that drew sword.
And the Philistines fought, and Israel was smitten, and they fled every man into his tent: and there was a very great slaughter; for there fell of Israel thirty thousand footmen.
corruption_summary: An honest old word for the infantryman; the corruption is an age that treats weariness as proof that the calling was wrong.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic instinct of our day answers Jeremiah's complaint the way God did not. Told that the footmen have wearied him, the modern counsellor lightens the load, renames the calling a poor fit, and treats fatigue itself as the verdict on a man's vocation. The LORD's answer runs the opposite way. He does not deny that the prophet is tired, and He does not scold him for saying so; He tells him plainly that horses are coming, and that the swelling of Jordan lies beyond the land of peace. That is not cruelty. It is the honesty of a Commander who intends His man to survive the real war, and who knows that a soldier flattered in the easy season is a soldier destroyed in the hard one.

The recovery is the biblical doctrine of endurance: strength is given for the race actually set, and it is given in the running, not before it. “They that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength… they shall run, and not be weary” (Isa 40:31), and the runner is bidden to “run with patience the race that is set before us, looking unto Jesus” (Heb 12:1–2). Note where the eyes go. Not to the length of the course and not inward to the state of one's own reserves, but to the Forerunner who ran the whole distance, contended with horses, went down into the swelling of Jordan, and came up on the other side. Jeremiah kept his post for forty more years on that answer.
roots_summary: Footman = the infantryman, the soldier on foot; Hebrew raglī, “one on foot.”
roots_lines: Footman — foot + man; the soldier who marches and fights afoot.
Hebrew raglī, from regel, the foot; opposed to the horseman and charioteer.
Not the liveried house-servant of later English — always a man of war in the AV.
Israel's armies are numbered in footmen (Num 11:21; Jdg 20:2; 1Sa 4:10).
Jer 12:5 makes the footrace the emblem of the lighter trial that trains a man for the heavier.
usage: If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee — then horses are coming.
God answers weariness not by shortening the course but by strengthening the runner.
A footman is the common man of the host — the rank God most often uses.

etymology: From horse and man, rendering the Hebrew pārāsh — a rider, and by extension the mounted arm of an army, the cavalry that ranked with the chariot as the terror of ancient war.
biblical_def: A horseman is a mounted soldier, and in Scripture he is almost always a picture of the strength of the nations — swift, costly, terrifying, and useless against God. Egypt is the first great cavalry power the Bible shows us, and the Bible shows her drowning: “the horse of Pharaoh went in with his chariots and with his horsemen into the sea, and the LORD brought again the waters of the sea upon them” (Exo 15:19). That deliverance set the doctrine for ever after. Israel was forbidden to multiply horses, and Isaiah pronounced the woe when she went shopping for them: “Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel” (Isa 31:1). David had already put the whole matter into a line a child can carry: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). Yet the word has a glorious other side. When Elijah was taken up, Elisha cried after him, “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof” (2Ki 2:12) — naming one praying prophet as worth more to the nation than all its cavalry. The true strength of a people is the men who stand before God for it.
webster_summary: A rider; a mounted soldier; the cavalry arm of an ancient army.
webster_full: HORSEMAN, a rider on horseback; a man skilled in riding; a soldier who serves on horseback.
From horse and man; Hebrew pārāsh, a rider or cavalryman.
The mounted arm ranked with the chariot as the chief military strength of the heathen nations.
Israel's kings were forbidden to multiply horses (Deu 17:16); Egypt's horsemen drowned in the sea.
Elisha calls Elijah himself the chariot of Israel and the horsemen thereof (2Ki 2:12).
scriptures: For the horse of Pharaoh went in with his chariots and with his horsemen into the sea, and the LORD brought again the waters of the sea upon them; but the children of Israel went on dry land in the midst of the sea.
Psa 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
Isa 31:1

Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the LORD!
And Elisha saw it, and he cried, My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof. And he saw him no more: and he took hold of his own clothes, and rent them in two pieces.
corruption_summary: The horsemen are gone; the trust in visible strength is not, and every age names its own cavalry.
corruption_paragraphs: No one now goes down to Egypt for horses, but every generation finds a mounted arm to lean on, and the church is not exempt. The modern horsemen are the platform, the funding, the political majority, the celebrity endorsement, the technology that promises reach without holiness. Isaiah's woe is not aimed at chariots as such; it is aimed at the look. Judah “look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the LORD” — the eyes went where the strength appeared to be, and the strength that was really there went unconsulted. That is the sin, and it is committed as easily in a boardroom as in a stable.

The recovery is not asceticism about means but a fixed order of trust. Psalm 20 does not say the godly own no horses; it says they do not trust them. The believer may plan, build, budget, and arm, and still say with David, “we will remember the name of the LORD our God” — and the proof of which way the heart leans comes on the day the horses are taken away. So Elisha's cry stands as the standing correction: the real cavalry of a nation is the man who prays and preaches and will not bend, and when God removes such a man, the defence is gone though every stable is full. “An horse is a vain thing for safety: neither shall he deliver any by his great strength” (Psa 33:17).
roots_summary: Horseman = a rider, a cavalryman; Hebrew pārāsh, the mounted arm of a host.
roots_lines: Horseman — horse + man; Hebrew pārāsh, a rider.
With the chariot, the chief military strength of Egypt, Syria, Assyria, and Babylon.
Israel's king was forbidden to multiply horses to himself (Deu 17:16).
Pharaoh's horsemen went into the sea and did not come out (Exo 15:19).
Elisha names Elijah the chariot of Israel and the horsemen thereof (2Ki 2:12).
usage: Some trust in chariots, and some in horses — and every age has its own cavalry.
Isaiah's woe falls not on the horses but on the look that goes to them instead of to God.
One praying prophet was the chariot and horsemen of a whole nation.

etymology: From armour (Old French armeure, from Latin armatura) and bearer. It renders the Hebrew phrase nōsē' kēlīm, “bearer of the vessels” — the young man who carried a warrior's shield and weapons and fought at his side.
biblical_def: An armourbearer is the young man attached to a captain or a king to carry his shield and weapons, to follow him into the press, and to finish what his master's stroke began. The office is a study in faithful subordinate service, and Scripture gives it two portraits, one bright and one black. The bright one is at Michmash. Jonathan proposes an act of pure faith — two men against a Philistine garrison — on the ground that “there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few” (1Sa 14:6), and his armourbearer answers with one of the finest sentences a servant ever spoke: “Do all that is in thine heart: turn thee; behold, I am with thee according to thy heart” (1Sa 14:7). He does not have the vision; he has the man who has it, and that is enough. So they climb on hands and feet, “and his armourbearer slew after him” (1Sa 14:13), and the LORD sent an earthquake and routed a host. The black portrait is on Gilboa, where Saul asks his armourbearer to run him through, and the young man will not, and then falls upon his own sword and dies with his master (1Sa 31:5). Loyalty is a great thing and it is not an ultimate thing. The servant who follows a faithful man follows him into victory; the servant who follows a rejected king follows him into the grave.
webster_summary: The attendant who carried a warrior's shield and weapons and fought beside him.
webster_full: ARMOURBEARER, he that bears the armour of another; the attendant of a warrior or captain.
Hebrew nōsē' kēlīm, “bearer of the vessels” or instruments of war.
He carried shield and weapons, followed his master into the fight, and despatched the wounded.
Jonathan's armourbearer at Michmash is the pattern of faithful subordinate service (1Sa 14:7).
David served as armourbearer to Saul before he served as his successor.
scriptures: And Jonathan said to the young man that bare his armour, Come, and let us go over unto the garrison of these uncircumcised: it may be that the LORD will work for us: for there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few.
And his armourbearer said unto him, Do all that is in thine heart: turn thee; behold, I am with thee according to thy heart.
And Jonathan climbed up upon his hands and upon his feet, and his armourbearer after him: and they fell before Jonathan; and his armourbearer slew after him.
And when his armourbearer saw that Saul was dead, he fell likewise upon his sword, and died with him.
corruption_summary: A word for faithful second-rank service; the corruption is an age that despises the second rank, and a church culture that makes loyalty to a man ultimate.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors sit on opposite sides of this word. The first is the contempt our age has for the second rank. Everyone is taught to be the visionary and no one to be the man who carries the shield, so churches fill with would-be Jonathans and starve for armourbearers — deacons, helpers, wives, sons, faithful members who will say to a called man, “I am with thee according to thy heart,” and then climb the rock behind him. Scripture gives that servant no name and gives him the whole victory: the LORD wrought a great deliverance that day by two men, and one of them was only a carrier of weapons. Hiddenness is not insignificance in the kingdom of God.

The second error runs the other way, and certain corners of evangelical teaching have built whole ministries on it — the “armourbearer” taught as unlimited loyalty to a pastor, obedience without examination, silence about a leader's sin as though the office covered the man. Gilboa is the answer. Saul's armourbearer was loyal to the end and the end was a suicide; his devotion to a rejected king could not save either of them. Christian submission to leaders is real (Heb 13:17) and it is never absolute, for every elder stands under the Word and the congregation is charged to try what he says by it (Act 17:11). Carry the shield gladly; follow the man only as far as he follows Christ.
roots_summary: Armourbearer = the attendant who carried a warrior's weapons and fought at his side.
roots_lines: Armourbearer — Hebrew nōsē' kēlīm, “bearer of the vessels” of war.
He bore the shield and weapons, followed into the press, and despatched the fallen.
Jonathan's at Michmash: “Do all that is in thine heart” (1Sa 14:7).
Saul's on Gilboa: loyal unto death, and the death was a rejected king's (1Sa 31:5).
Abimelech and Joab also had armourbearers; David bore Saul's before he wore his crown.
usage: I am with thee according to thy heart — the armourbearer's whole creed.
The kingdom is short not of visionaries but of men who will carry the shield.
Loyalty is a great virtue and never an ultimate one; Gilboa proves it.

etymology: From captain (Old French capitain, from Latin caput, head) and fifty. It renders the Hebrew sar 'hāmishshīm — a junior officer over a company of fifty men, the lowest of the graded commands Jethro set up in Exodus 18.
biblical_def: The captain of fifty is a junior officer — the lowest rung of the graded command Jethro counselled Moses to appoint, “rulers of thousands, and rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens” (Exo 18:21). He is a real rank in Israel's civil and military order, and Isaiah lists him among the props God threatens to pull out from under Judah: “The captain of fifty, and the honourable man, and the counsellor” (Isa 3:3). But he is remembered for one narrative. Ahaziah, injured and enquiring of Baalzebub, sends soldiers to fetch Elijah down from his hill. The first comes with a summons in his mouth: “Thou man of God, the king hath said, Come down” (2Ki 1:9) — and fire falls. The second comes the same way, and fire falls again. Then comes the third, and everything changes, not in the rank but in the man: “the third captain of fifty went up, and came and fell on his knees before Elijah, and besought him, and said unto him, O man of God, I pray thee, let my life, and the life of these fifty thy servants, be precious in thy sight” (2Ki 1:13). He had seen what happened to the two before him, and he drew the right conclusion (2Ki 1:14). Here is the whole difference between summoning God and beseeching Him. The two who commanded the prophet died; the one who begged lived, and his fifty with him.
webster_summary: A junior officer set over a company of fifty men; the lowest of Israel's graded commands.
webster_full: CAPTAIN OF FIFTY, an officer commanding a company of fifty men.
Hebrew sar 'hāmishshīm; the least of the ranks of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens (Exo 18:21).
A standing rank in Israel's civil and military order, and in the king's guard.
Isaiah names him among the stays of the state that God threatens to remove (Isa 3:3).
Three such captains were sent to Elijah; two were consumed and the third was spared (2Ki 1).
scriptures: Then the king sent unto him a captain of fifty with his fifty. And he went up to him: and, behold, he sat on the top of an hill. And he spake unto him, Thou man of God, the king hath said, Come down.

And he sent again a captain of the third fifty with his fifty. And the third captain of fifty went up, and came and fell on his knees before Elijah, and besought him, and said unto him, O man of God, I pray thee, let my life, and the life of these fifty thy servants, be precious in thy sight.
Behold, there came fire down from heaven, and burnt up the two captains of the former fifties with their fifties: therefore let my life now be precious in thy sight.
Isa 3:3
The captain of fifty, and the honourable man, and the counsellor, and the cunning artificer, and the eloquent orator.
corruption_summary: A minor rank with a major lesson; the corruption is the modern habit of approaching God as a superior officer issues an order.
corruption_paragraphs: Ahaziah's captains carry the king's tone into the presence of the LORD's prophet, and the tone is the sin. “The king hath said, Come down” — a summons, a schedule, an expectation of compliance. Whole streams of modern religion have institutionalised exactly that posture: the word of faith teacher who instructs the believer to decree and declare, to command his healing, to call things into being as though the creature had the Creator's prerogative; the practical deism of the man who prays as one files a requisition and is offended when it is not filled. The name of God has been made a lever. Fire from heaven is the biblical estimate of that error, and it fell twice before the lesson took.

The third captain is the corrective, and he is not a better man — he is a wiser one. He climbs the same hill on the same errand under the same king, but he comes on his knees and asks that his life be precious in the prophet's sight, and he goes down alive with his fifty behind him. That is how sinners come to God: not summoning but beseeching, not decreeing but pleading, casting themselves on a mercy they cannot compel. “God be merciful to me a sinner” is the third captain's prayer in the temple, and the LORD who would not be commanded off His hill has never yet refused a man who came up it on his knees.
roots_summary: Captain of fifty = a junior officer over fifty men; Hebrew sar 'hāmishshīm.
roots_lines: Captain of fifty — Latin caput, head; the head of a company of fifty.
The lowest of Jethro's four grades: thousands, hundreds, fifties, tens (Exo 18:21).
A distinct rank from the captain of the host, who commanded an entire army.
Isaiah lists him among the stays God will take away from Judah (Isa 3:3).
Two such captains commanded Elijah and were consumed; the third besought him and lived.
usage: The king hath said, Come down — and fire came down instead.
Two captains summoned the prophet and died; the third besought him and lived.
The rank never changed; the knees did.

etymology: From the Anglo-Saxon sinu, a tendon — the tough cord that binds muscle to bone. It renders the Hebrew gīd, the tendon or nerve, and figuratively the stiffness or strength of a thing.
biblical_def: A sinew is a tendon — the tough white cord that ties muscle to bone and makes a limb obey. Scripture puts the word at three great moments. The first is Peniel. Jacob wrestles till the breaking of the day with a Man who is no man, and when He sees that He prevails not, “he touched the hollow of his thigh; and the hollow of Jacob's thigh was out of joint” (Gen 32:25). One touch ended the contest. Israel went out of that night with a new name and a limp, and his sons remember it in their diet to this day: “the children of Israel eat not of the sinew which shrank, which is upon the hollow of the thigh” (Gen 32:32). The mark of the man who prevailed with God is a shrunken tendon. He prevailed exactly when he was crippled, and thereafter he clung because he could no longer wrestle. The second moment is in the valley of dry bones, where sinews are the first thing the LORD promises to a scattered nation: “I will lay sinews upon you, and will bring up flesh upon you… and ye shall live” (Eze 37:6) — though sinew and flesh and skin come up and there is still no breath in them until the Spirit is called. The third is Isaiah's indictment of the same people unhumbled: “thy neck is an iron sinew, and thy brow brass” (Isa 48:4). Stiff sinew or shrunken sinew: God will have one or the other.
webster_summary: A tendon; the cord binding muscle to bone — figuratively, strength or stiffness.
webster_full: SINEW, a tendon; that which unites a muscle to a bone; in a figurative sense, strength or that which supplies strength.
From the Saxon sinu; Hebrew gīd, a tendon or nerve.
Jacob's thigh-sinew shrank at Peniel, and Israel abstains from it still (Gen 32:32).
Ezekiel's dry bones are clothed with sinews before breath enters them (Eze 37:6).
An iron sinew in the neck is Isaiah's figure for obstinacy (Isa 48:4).
scriptures: Therefore the children of Israel eat not of the sinew which shrank, which is upon the hollow of the thigh, unto this day: because he touched the hollow of Jacob's thigh in the sinew that shrank.
And when he saw that he prevailed not against him, he touched the hollow of his thigh; and the hollow of Jacob's thigh was out of joint, as he wrestled with him.
Eze 37:6
And I will lay sinews upon you, and will bring up flesh upon you, and cover you with skin, and put breath in you, and ye shall live; and ye shall know that I am the LORD.
Isa 48:4
Because I knew that thou art obstinate, and thy neck is an iron sinew, and thy brow brass;
corruption_summary: A word for the body's tough cordage; the live misuse is a religion of strengthened sinews that has never been touched and made to limp.
corruption_paragraphs: The message the natural heart wants from religion is reinforcement — stronger sinews, firmer resolve, a better grip. Whole shelves of Christian publishing offer it: principles for the man who wants to prevail, keys, disciplines, the seven habits of the overcomer. Peniel is the standing rebuke of that whole genre. Jacob was the strongest wrestler in Scripture and he was beaten by a touch, and it was after the touch, hanging on a dislocated hip with no strength left to grapple, that he said “I will not let thee go, except thou bless me” and heard himself renamed Israel. The blessing came to the cripple. God does not make prevailing men by thickening their sinews; He makes them by shrinking one, so that clinging is all that is left.

The recovery is the doctrine Paul learned in the same school: “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness” (2Co 12:9). This is not a comfort for the feeble only; it is the ordinary way God deals with strong men, and the limp is not a defect in the Christian life but the signature of it. And the valley of dry bones guards the point from the other side: sinews upon the bones are not life. Israel got tendon and flesh and skin and lay there a corpse until the Spirit was commanded to breathe. Reformation of the frame is not regeneration. What raises the dead is not sinew but the sovereign breath of God, and that is monergism written in bone.
roots_summary: Sinew = a tendon; Hebrew gīd — and figuratively the strength or stiffness of a man.
roots_lines: Sinew — Saxon sinu, a tendon; Hebrew gīd, tendon or nerve.
Peniel: the sinew that shrank when the Man touched Jacob's thigh (Gen 32:25, 32).
Israel's abstinence from that sinew keeps the memory of the night in the nation's diet.
Ezekiel 37: sinews laid on dry bones — frame before breath, and breath is the Spirit.
Isaiah 48:4: an iron sinew in the neck is stubbornness against God.
usage: The mark of the man who prevailed with God was a shrunken sinew and a limp.
Sinew on dry bones is a body, not a life; the breath must come from God.
An iron sinew in the neck is not strength but obstinacy.

etymology: From the Anglo-Saxon flint, a hard quartz stone that strikes fire and fractures to a cutting edge. It renders the Hebrew halmīsh and tsōr, the flinty rock — the byword in Scripture for whatever is hardest.
biblical_def: Flint is the hardest common stone of the land — the rock that strikes fire, splits to a knife-edge, and yields to nothing. Scripture turns it three ways. First it is the emblem of God's power over the impossible. Moses reminds Israel of the wilderness “where there was no water; who brought thee forth water out of the rock of flint” (Deu 8:15), and the psalmist sings of the God “which turned the rock into a standing water, the flint into a fountain of waters” (Psa 114:8). The hardest thing in creation becomes a spring at His word, which is the pledge to every man who despairs of a hard heart — his own or another's. Second, flint is the figure of holy resolve. The Servant of the LORD says, “The Lord GOD will help me; therefore shall I not be confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be ashamed” (Isa 50:7) — a prophecy Luke reports fulfilled when Christ “stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luk 9:51), knowing the cross was at the end of that road. Third, flint arms the prophet: “As an adamant harder than flint have I made thy forehead: fear them not, neither be dismayed at their looks” (Eze 3:9). God gives His messengers a brow harder than the faces set against them. Hard rock, softened; soft hearts, hardened for duty. Both are His work.
webster_summary: A very hard quartz stone that strikes fire and splits to an edge; the proverbial figure for hardness or resolve.
webster_full: FLINT, a very hard siliceous stone, striking fire with steel; used for knives and for arrow-heads before the age of metal.
Figuratively, anything of extreme hardness or firmness; a hard heart, or an unyielding purpose.
Hebrew halmīsh and tsōr, the flinty rock of the wilderness.
The LORD brought water out of the rock of flint for Israel (Deu 8:15; Psa 114:8).
The Servant sets His face like a flint and is not ashamed (Isa 50:7).
scriptures: Deu 8:15
Who led thee through that great and terrible wilderness, wherein were fiery serpents, and scorpions, and drought, where there was no water; who brought thee forth water out of the rock of flint;
Isa 50:7
For the Lord GOD will help me; therefore shall I not be confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be ashamed.
Eze 3:9
As an adamant harder than flint have I made thy forehead: fear them not, neither be dismayed at their looks, though they be a rebellious house.
Which turned the rock into a standing water, the flint into a fountain of waters.
corruption_summary: A hard stone made a figure for holy resolve; the corruption is an age that mistakes every firmness for cruelty and calls softness love.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning sentiment holds that a set face is a closed mind and that firmness is a failure of compassion — so the pastor who will not move is called rigid, the father who will not bend the rule is called cold, and the church that keeps a boundary is charged with lacking love. Isaiah 50 destroys the equation. The face set like a flint in that chapter is the face of the Suffering Servant, and the very next verse shows what He set it toward: the smiters, the pluckers of the beard, the shame and the spitting. That flint was not hardness against men; it was hardness against turning back from a road that led to a cross for men. The most resolved face in Scripture belongs to the most compassionate Person in Scripture, and the two are one act.

So the recovery runs on two lines that Scripture holds together and the age holds apart. God hardens what must not yield — the prophet's forehead against a rebellious house, the Servant's face toward Jerusalem, the believer's purpose against the pull of the world. And God softens what must not stay hard: the flint becomes a fountain, and that miracle is precisely the promise of the new covenant, “I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh” (Eze 36:26). A man's heart is flint by nature and cannot soften itself; a man's face is water by nature and cannot set itself. Sovereign grace does both, and does them in the same soul.
roots_summary: Flint = the hardest common stone — and Scripture's figure both for what God softens and for the resolve He gives.
roots_lines: Flint — Saxon flint; Hebrew halmīsh, tsōr, the flinty rock.
It strikes fire with steel and fractures to a cutting edge; used for knives before metal.
Water from the rock of flint is the wilderness proof of God's power (Deu 8:15; Psa 114:8).
A face set like a flint is unbending purpose (Isa 50:7; fulfilled Luk 9:51).
A forehead as adamant harder than flint is the prophet's armour (Eze 3:9).
usage: He set his face like a flint — and the road it was set toward ended at Calvary.
The flint became a fountain: no heart is too hard for the God who did that.
God hardens the prophet's brow and softens the sinner's heart, and both are grace.

etymology: From the Old French tempeste, from Latin tempestas, “a season, weather, storm” (from tempus, time). In the Authorized Version it renders several Hebrew and Greek words for a violent storm of wind, rain, or hail.
biblical_def: A tempest is a violent storm — wind, sea, and sky turned against a man — and in Scripture it is never merely weather. It is one of the LORD's instruments, sent, aimed, and stilled at His pleasure. David, hunted and betrayed by his familiar friend, longs for wings to be gone: “I would hasten my escape from the windy storm and tempest” (Psa 55:8). Jonah meets the same word going the other way, and there it is unmistakably a summons: “the LORD sent out a great wind into the sea, and there was a mighty tempest in the sea, so that the ship was like to be broken” (Jon 1:4). The heathen mariners cast lots and the lot found the prophet, and Jonah at last owned it — “for I know that for my sake this great tempest is upon you” (Jon 1:12). A tempest may be the chastening of a runaway saint before it is anything else. The word rises highest in Hebrews, where Sinai is summed up in it: the mount that burned with fire, “nor unto blackness, and darkness, and tempest” (Heb 12:18) — the storm of the law, which the believer has not come to. He is come instead to mount Sion and to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant. Isaiah names where the shelter is: “a man shall be… a covert from the tempest” (Isa 32:2). That Man is Christ.
webster_summary: A violent storm of wind, rain, or hail; figuratively any violent commotion or tumult.
webster_full: TEMPEST, an extensive current of wind, rushing with great velocity and violence; a storm of extreme violence.
From the Latin tempestas, weather or storm, from tempus, time or season.
Figuratively, any violent tumult or commotion of a nation, a household, or a soul.
In Scripture the tempest is sent, governed, and stilled by the LORD (Jon 1:4).
Sinai itself is summed up as blackness, darkness, and tempest (Heb 12:18).
scriptures: Psa 55:8
I would hasten my escape from the windy storm and tempest.
Jon 1:4
But the LORD sent out a great wind into the sea, and there was a mighty tempest in the sea, so that the ship was like to be broken.
Jon 1:12
And he said unto them, Take me up, and cast me forth into the sea; so shall the sea be calm unto you: for I know that for my sake this great tempest is upon you.
For ye are not come unto the mount that might be touched, and that burned with fire, nor unto blackness, and darkness, and tempest,
corruption_summary: A word for the storm God sends; the corruption is the deism that grants Him the calm and denies Him the gale.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern religion is content to say that God is with us in the storm and stops carefully short of saying that He sent it. The weather becomes a blind system, the affliction becomes a random misfortune, and God is reduced to a sympathetic companion who happens to be present at a disaster He did not order. Scripture will not have it. “The LORD sent out a great wind into the sea” — sent it, with a runaway prophet in the hold and a course to change; and the God who has “his way in the whirlwind and in the storm” (Nah 1:3) is not a bystander to His own creation. A providence with the tempests removed from it is not a comfort; it is an idol, and it collapses the moment a real gale blows.

The recovery is the doctrine of sovereign providence held with both hands. The same LORD who sent the tempest upon Jonah prepared the fish that saved him, and the storm was mercy in a terrible dress — it drove a fleeing prophet back to his commission and gave a shipload of heathen mariners the fear of the true God. Jonah's three days in the deep are the sign Christ claimed for His own burial (Mat 12:40), and this is where the doctrine lands: the tempest of the law at Sinai and the tempest of divine wrath both broke over Christ, and the believer who is in Him is not come unto blackness and darkness and tempest but unto Jesus. Isaiah promised a covert from the tempest, and He is standing in the storm.
roots_summary: Tempest = a violent storm — Latin tempestas, weather; in Scripture, sent and governed by the LORD.
roots_lines: Tempest — Old French tempeste, Latin tempestas, from tempus, time or season.
Renders several Hebrew and Greek words for storm of wind, rain, or hail.
David longs to escape the windy storm and tempest of treachery (Psa 55:8).
Jonah's tempest was sent by name, and he owned it as his own (Jon 1:4, 12).
Hebrews sums up Sinai as blackness, darkness, and tempest — not the believer's mount (Heb 12:18).
usage: For my sake this great tempest is upon you — a runaway prophet at last telling the truth.
God does not merely accompany the storm; He sends it, aims it, and stills it.
Ye are not come unto blackness, and darkness, and tempest — but unto Jesus.
